transcript.text: Hey, Alex. I own a coffee shop. I tried
going off grid for 7 days to see if the
business could run without me. Didn't
even make it to day three. I realized
I'm the process for about half the
things that happen in my shop. If I get
hit by a bus, the whole thing falls
apart. What do I do and where do I even
start? Good question.
Two things.
First, you'll do something called a time
study, which basically means you set a
timer every 15 minutes throughout the
day. It can be your watch, it can be an
iPhone, it doesn't matter. And whenever
it goes off, you open an Excel sheet and
you have the times per day and you write
down what you were doing or what you did
in the last 15 minutes. It feels like
it's going to be a massive distraction.
It's not. Because what it's going to do
is give you full transparency into where
your time is going. Once you have a week
or two weeks, I want you to go back and
look at all those times and the actions
that you were taking and say, is there a
process, a person, or a project that I
need to create to resolve this thing?
And when we look at that whole mess of
work that you're doing, there's going to
be something that's the lowest ROI that
can be done with a process or an
automation and we're going to start with
those first. And then you're going to
have the second lowest ROI and maybe
it's a process or a project. I want to
get all my process and projects off my
plate that are the lowest ROI first, so
I create more room. After that, I'm
going to look at the ones that I think
people are going to be solving. And so
then I would solve it with people. And
all you're doing fundamentally is buying
back your time. I think where you get
stuck is when you try to buy everything
back at once with one person. It almost
never works because that's expecting
someone to have lived your entire life
and have all the skills as you on their
second day. So the key to getting your
time back is getting it back drop by
drop, not all at once.
